title: Septic Shock — Resuscitation Targets
sources: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 — International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock (Intensive Care Med 2026; Crit Care Med 2026) — updates the 2021 guideline with 129 statements (46 new); currency review confirmed this module's existing trial-based content already anticipated most of the 2026 direction, with peripheral-vasopressor timing, age-adjusted MAP, and broadened corticosteroid use as the specific updates applied here.
Hernandez G et al. 25 years of septic shock hemodynamic resuscitation trials. Crit Care 2026;30:400
ADRENAL (NEJM 2018;378:797); APROCCHSS (NEJM 2018;378:809) — corticosteroids in septic shock, mixed mortality signal across trials

changelog.change: Currency update to SSC 2026: broadened the hydrocortisone recommendation from 'shock not responding to fluids + moderate-dose norepinephrine' to any septic shock requiring vasopressor support (2026 no longer gates it to a dose threshold, though the mortality evidence across ADRENAL/APROCCHSS remains mixed — framed as a reasonable-to-start conditional recommendation, not a mandate). Added the age ≥ 65 lower MAP target (60-65 mmHg) to the MAP section. Cross-linked venous-congestion-deresuscitation explicitly in the de-resuscitation bullet and in `related`. The peripheral-vasopressor line was already current (SSC 2021 carried it, SSC 2026 keeps and reinforces it) — citation updated.
Added whyThisMatters + clinicalTakeaway (standard Reference Library template, DIRECTIONS_FORWARD §1).

Initial entry — bedside resuscitation targets and titration sequence for septic shock, distilled from SSC 2021 + the ANDROMEDA-SHOCK line + the 25-year conceptual review. Management-oriented (what to titrate to what), not a trial summary.

summary: Antibiotics + source control within the hour. Resuscitate to perfusion, not to a single number: MAP ≥ 65, CRT normalizing, lactate clearing, mentation and urine output improving, falling pressor requirement. After the initial bolus, test fluid responsiveness before every further bolus.
whyThisMatters: Septic shock kills through time and under-resuscitation: every hour antibiotics are delayed raises mortality, and the commonest bedside error is chasing one number — a MAP, a CVP, a lactate — instead of the patient's actual perfusion. The opposite error is just as lethal: pouring fluid into a patient who has stopped responding to it. Recognition and antibiotics belong to the ED; hemodynamic titration and de-resuscitation continue in the ICU.
clinicalTakeaway: Antibiotics and source control within the first hour. Then resuscitate to perfusion, not to one dial — MAP ≥ 65 with a normalizing capillary refill, clearing lactate, improving mentation and urine output, and a falling pressor requirement. After the first bolus, prove fluid responsiveness before every further bolus, and stop when the patient stops responding.

items: Blood cultures ×2 (don't delay antibiotics for them), lactate, then broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 h of recognition — see the empiric-antibiotics modules.
Identify and address the source in parallel (imaging, drainage, debridement, line removal).
Initial fluid: ~30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid (LR / Plasma-Lyte over saline in sepsis) for hypotension or lactate ≥ 4, then STOP and reassess. Not a fixed prescription to repeat.

Start norepinephrine early — through a peripheral IV rather than delaying for a central line (SSC 2021, reinforced in SSC 2026). In unstable shock, starting fluid and a vasopressor concurrently rather than sequentially is reasonable rather than waiting to see if fluid alone works first. Target MAP ≥ 65 (see the age-adjusted nuance below).

body.text: Default MAP ≥ 65 mmHg. SSC 2026 suggests a lower initial target of 60–65 mmHg for patients ≥ 65 years old, to limit cumulative vasopressor exposure in a group where that exposure itself carries risk — this is a floor to start from, not a ceiling; titrate up if perfusion markers don't improve. A higher target (80–85) gave no overall mortality or renal benefit and caused more new-onset atrial fibrillation (SEPSISPAM) — reserve it for chronic hypertensives, where the higher target reduced RRT need without the AF penalty. Titrate to the individual: mentation, urine output, CRT, and lactate trend matter more than the number.

rows: First-line. No true max — but a rising requirement is a trigger to add a second agent, not just to keep climbing.
Add EARLY as the second agent rather than escalating norepinephrine alone (catecholamine-sparing). Not weight-based.

IV, continuous infusion or 50 mg q6h. SSC 2026 broadens this to any septic shock requiring ongoing vasopressor support, rather than gating it to a specific dose threshold — but the mortality evidence itself is genuinely mixed (ADRENAL: faster shock reversal, no mortality benefit; APROCCHSS: a mortality benefit with hydrocortisone+fludrocortisone together), so treat it as reasonable-to-start rather than a mandate, and stop it once vasopressors are off.
If echo or clinical picture shows sepsis-related myocardial dysfunction with persistent hypoperfusion despite adequate MAP and preload (~40% of septic shock).

body.text: See the pressor-inotrope reference for mixing recipes and the full hemodynamic table. Refractory vasoplegia rescue tier: methylene blue → hydroxocobalamin.
Fluid — after the initial bolus, test before you give

items: Do NOT give reflexive repeat boluses. Before each additional bolus, demonstrate fluid responsiveness: passive leg raise with a real-time cardiac-output monitor, a 4-mL/kg fluid challenge, or pulse-pressure / stroke-volume variation ≥ 12% in a passive, ventilated, sinus-rhythm patient.
Systematic fluid-responsiveness testing before any bolus avoided fluid entirely in ~25% of patients in ANDROMEDA-SHOCK.

A restrictive strategy is safe (CLASSIC). Also weigh fluid TOLERANCE — rising CVP, IVC plethora, B-lines, portal-vein pulsatility (VExUS) — not just responsiveness. A responsive but congested patient does not need more fluid.

Once stabilized, shift to de-resuscitation: aim for a neutral-to-negative fluid balance, remove accumulated fluid, and watch for venous congestion / organ edema — SSC 2026 formalizes active fluid removal after the initial resuscitation phase as its own step, not just an afterthought once the patient looks overloaded. See venous-congestion-deresuscitation for the VExUS grading and the full bedside de-resuscitation protocol.

body.text: Perfusion targets — treat the patient, not one dial

items: Capillary refill time: normalize it (≤ 3 s). Reassess every ~30 min in the first 8 h. CRT-targeted resuscitation performed at least as well as lactate-targeted with less fluid and organ dysfunction (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK) and shortened the duration of vital support in the phenotype-driven version (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2).

Lactate: a trajectory marker and a refractory-shock criterion, most informative in the first 6–12 h. Kinetics are biphasic — after the early window, persistent hyperlactatemia is increasingly driven by non-hypoxic causes (adrenergic aerobic glycolysis, impaired hepatic clearance, mitochondrial dysfunction). Do NOT keep escalating fluid and pressors to chase a lactate that stays high once CRT, mentation, urine output, and the pressor requirement have improved.
Also track: mental status, urine output, skin mottling, and the direction of the vasopressor requirement.

body.text: When shock persists despite the above, a structured bedside re-assessment sorts the patient into one dominant problem, each with a different next move:

rows: Fluid-responsive (PLR / PPV positive), small hyperdynamic LV, collapsing IVC
A titrated fluid challenge, then re-test
Low diastolic arterial pressure, wide pulse pressure, warm periphery, NOT fluid-responsive
Up-titrate norepinephrine to the DAP / MAP target; add vasopressin
Depressed LV/RV on echo, elevated filling pressures, cool periphery despite adequate MAP

items: ScvO2 as a resuscitation target — dropped from SSC guidance (both low and supranormal values associate with worse outcomes).
A fixed elevated CVP target and liberal transfusion thresholds (the old EGDT algorithm) — contradicted by later fluid-overload and transfusion data.
A persistently high lactate after the early window, once other perfusion markers have normalized.
A single MAP number for every patient regardless of premorbid blood pressure.
A normal glucose. Intensive control (80–110) increases mortality (NICE-SUGAR) — target ≤ 180 mg/dL.
A high-normal hemoglobin. Transfuse at a threshold of 7 g/dL in septic shock (TRISS); a liberal Hgb-9 trigger gave no benefit.

rows: No benefit over good usual care — the bundle is not the mechanism
Balanced crystalloid; albumin has no routine benefit (and is harmful in TBI)
Fluid strategy after the initial bolus
Restrictive is safe — favor testing responsiveness over volume
Vasopressin 0.03 U/min as a catecholamine-sparing adjunct, not a norepinephrine replacement
Normalize CRT; equal-or-better outcomes vs lactate-guided with less fluid
